claims.text: Integrating the Z method or a machine-learning-accelerated variant with DFT can predict melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change in refractory materials.
The resulting predictions will be reliable and close to those obtained by full thermodynamic integration.
The initial material state is a high-temperature refractory solid approaching melting.
Constant-energy DFT or ML-accelerated molecular dynamics can induce a superheated state followed by collapse into a liquid.
A microcanonical simulation permits observation of superheating followed by rapid collapse into the liquid state.
The appearance of a superheated metastable state and its sudden collapse are evidenced by discontinuities in energy and volume.
The superheated metastable state and collapse link the simulation dynamics to melting thermodynamic quantities.
Heating under constant energy causes the system to reach a superheated state.
Loss of metastability causes the superheated solid to collapse into a liquid phase.
Monitoring energy and volume changes during collapse provides a direct estimate of melting temperature.
Monitoring the collapse provides latent heat from which fusion enthalpy and entropy can be calculated.
Monitoring volume during collapse provides the volume change at melting.
The Z method will produce melting properties with reasonable accuracy relative to full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The Z method will reduce computational overhead sufficiently to enable high-throughput evaluations.
Ab initio free-energy calculations using thermodynamic integration through molecular dynamics are accurate.
Ab initio thermodynamic integration through molecular dynamics is computationally very expensive.
The approach is expected to work reliably for refractory systems in which superheating and abrupt collapse can be clearly resolved.
Accuracy may be limited for gradual phase transitions or systems with significant kinetic barriers.
Predicted latent heat and volume discontinuities may be sensitive to simulation parameters and subject to systematic deviations.

contradictions.description: The simulations are specified as constant-total-energy trajectories, but the mechanism says that the system is heated under constant energy without explaining that different initial energies or separate trajectories would be required.

The hypothesis invokes an energy discontinuity during a constant-total-energy simulation. This is internally inconsistent unless 'energy' is restricted to a component such as potential energy, which is not stated.
